statement.description: What the design lets a person do or understand, in one sentence.

measure.description: The observable outcome (a task completed in N steps, a state readable at a glance, a review that passes), not an adjective.

problem_evidence.title: Problem and evidence
problem_evidence.description: Each claim about the current experience with the source that shows it (a screenshot, a session, an issue, a document slug).

visual_direction.title: Visual direction
visual_direction.description: The chosen look and structure: layout, hierarchy, tokens, tone.

alternatives_considered.title: Alternatives considered
alternatives_considered.description: Other visual or interaction options, each shown (link, sketch, or description) with why it lost.

reference.description: Link, file path or document slug of the picture or prototype.

states.title: States and screens
states.description: Each state the design must show: empty, loading, error, partial, full.

rules.title: Rules
rules.description: Each design rule with an example that agrees with scope and acceptance criteria.

refusals.title: Refusals and exceptions
refusals.description: Every input or state the interface refuses or shows as an error, with message. Each needs an acceptance criterion that triggers it.

rule_changes.title: Rule changes
rule_changes.description: Existing design rules this changes. Each needs an acceptance criterion that pins the new behaviour.

human_acceptance.title: Acceptance by a human
human_acceptance.description: What a person must look at or try before this counts as done.

practice.description: What an established product does for this interaction.

difference.description: How this design differs and why.

dimensions.question: What does the design show for deleted or renamed items, for empty or vacuous sets ("all of zero items"), and for the first visit versus a repeated one?
Which refusals, errors or exceptions does the interface show, and which acceptance criterion triggers each one?
What does a person see when two sessions or people change the same thing at once? No answer may rely on exclusivity.
Which inputs can the design not observe (config, environment, files loaded by path, other processes), and how does the interface treat them?
Do the rule statements and their examples match the scope and the acceptance criteria?
Does anything here (a stopgap, a transitional screen, a hard-coded list, a fallback) become unnecessary under the end-state design? Where a list is needed, where does its single source live?
Does anything fail silently? What does the person see when a step cannot run?
For each acceptance criterion, what is the simplest wrong implementation that would still pass, and how does the criterion refuse it?
What is the render, load and token cost under load, and what bounds it?
How do existing screens, stored data and habits reach the new design?
Which alternatives were shown side by side (not only described), and why did the chosen one win?
How does it work with keyboard and screen reader, in both colour themes, and at phone width?
Which part needs a human to judge it, and what do they check?
